raw_text:
Transcaval access is a deliberately created, temporary aortocaval conduit that permits large-bore retrograde arterial device delivery from the femoral vein when conventional transfemoral arterial access is unsafe or impossible. Its clinical relevance has paralleled the expansion of transcatheter aortic valve replacement (TAVR), from first-in-human therapy to randomized evidence across inoperable, high-, intermediate-, and low-risk aortic stenosis populations [1-6]. Although contemporary delivery systems have become smaller and national registry data show that transfemoral access now predominates, a clinically important minority of patients retain hostile iliofemoral anatomy because of small caliber, circumferential calcification, tortuosity, prior surgery, or occlusive peripheral artery disease [7]. These same features are associated with vascular injury, bleeding, transfusion, and mortality after TAVR, making safe alternative access central to structural heart programs [8,9].

The conceptual basis of transcaval access was established in animal work showing that intentional caval-to-aortic traversal and closure could be tolerated even with large sheaths [10]. The key physiologic insight is counterintuitive: an aortic hole adjacent to a caval hole does not necessarily cause free retroperitoneal hemorrhage because the retroperitoneal space pressurizes and preferentially decompresses arterial bleeding into the low-pressure vena cava. The first human series demonstrated that caval-aortic access could enable TAVR in patients otherwise considered ineligible for available access routes, with high technical success but frequent transfusion and residual aortocaval flow [11].

Technique and imaging are inseparable. Preprocedural computed tomography is used to identify a calcium-free target on the right lateral abdominal aorta, avoid bowel or major venous/arterial structures, define fluoroscopic working angles and vertebral landmarks, and plan covered-stent bailout [12,13]. In the classic technique, a 0.014-inch guidewire within a coaxial catheter system is directed from the inferior vena cava toward an aortic snare and energized with electrosurgery to cross into the aorta. The wire is snared, exchanged for a stiff rail, and a large-bore sheath is advanced from the femoral vein into the abdominal aorta for standard retrograde structural intervention. At case completion, the tract is closed most often with an off-label nitinol occluder; protamine reversal, completion angiography, readiness for balloon tamponade, and availability of a covered stent are mandatory safeguards [12,13].

Prospective multicenter experience clarified the risk profile. In the NHLBI investigational study, transcaval access was successful in 99 of 100 attempted patients and enabled TAVR in a cohort without good femoral or transthoracic options, although bleeding, transfusion, and vascular complications remained relevant early hazards [14]. Importantly, 12-month follow-up showed no late transcaval vascular complications, no device migration or fracture, and near-universal spontaneous closure of residual aortocaval fistulae on computed tomography [15]. A purpose-built transcaval closure device subsequently improved immediate hemostasis in first-in-human testing, suggesting that dedicated technology may reduce bleeding and lower the barrier to broader dissemination [16]. Technical refinements, including laser-assisted crossing in heavily calcified targets, have expanded procedural options but should be confined to highly experienced teams [17].

Comparative data remain observational. A propensity-weighted contemporary analysis from experienced U.S. centers found lower stroke or transient ischemic attack after transcaval than transaxillary TAVR, with similar major bleeding, transfusion, vascular complications, and survival [18]. Best-practice recommendations emphasize that favorable outcomes depend on rigorous CT planning, standard equipment checklists, proctorship, clear bailout algorithms, and honest recognition of unsuitable anatomy [19]. More recent single-center experience suggests that radial rather than femoral secondary arterial access may be feasible in selected transcaval TAVI cases, though this limits immediate covered-stent bailout and therefore demands careful patient selection [20].

Although TAVR is the dominant structural application, transcaval access is better viewed as a large-bore aortic access platform. It has been used to deliver high-flow Impella 5.0 support in cardiogenic shock when femoral arterial access is inadequate, allowing percutaneous support while avoiding limb ischemia [21]. It has also enabled thoracic endovascular aortic repair in patients without suitable iliofemoral arteries, including reports using conventional fluoroscopic or intravascular ultrasound guidance [22,23]. Surgical and endovascular reviews therefore frame transcaval access as a bridge between interventional cardiology and vascular surgery, valuable when large devices must reach the aorta but arterial routes are exhausted [24].

The evidence base is still limited by small cohorts, referral bias, and concentration in expert centers. Recent meta-analyses, however, report high procedural success and acceptable short-term mortality, bleeding, vascular complication, and stroke rates compared with other alternative-access strategies [25,26]. In practice, transcaval access should be considered after a heart team evaluates transfemoral optimization, intravascular lithotripsy, transcarotid, transaxillary/subclavian, and transthoracic routes [27-29]. Outcomes should be reported with standardized Valve Academic Research Consortium definitions to support meaningful comparison across access strategies [30]. For selected patients with prohibitive iliofemoral arterial disease, transcaval access offers a fully percutaneous, transfemoral-ergonomic route for structural heart intervention; its future depends on training, dedicated closure systems, and multicenter comparative data.
